proof_summary: Letting \(s\) be the digit sum of \(n\), remove the factors \(2\) and \(5\) from \(s\), choose a fixed block width via Euler’s theorem, and concatenate suitably many blocks representing \(1\) and \(10\); a linear congruence makes the resulting number divisible by \(s\), while every block has digit sum \(1\), so its total digit sum is \(n\). Appending enough trailing zeros restores the removed factors and makes the number a positive multiple of \(10\); it cannot equal \(n\), since a positive multiple of \(10\) has digit sum strictly smaller than itself.
